# symbolic

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/symbolic)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=symbolic)
<!-- badges: end -->

`symbolic` is an R package designed to provide symbolic algebra capabilities natively in R using R functions.


It is highly experimental and dependent on external contributors to be a fully fledged Computer Algebra System (CAS). It will be developed to the extent needed for my upstream packages, specifically distributional which requires many symbolic algebra tools not yet readily available in R. Currently powered by [Maxima](https://maxima.sourceforge.io/), embedded in R via the [maxima](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/maxima) package.


## Installation

You can install the development version of symbolic like so:

``` r
remotes::install_github("mitchelloharawild/symbolic")
```

This also installs the [maxima](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/maxima)
package, which compiles Maxima (and the ECL Lisp it runs on) from source. No
system installation of Maxima is needed, but the first install takes a while.

## Usage

Prepare a function for symbolic transformations with `as_symbolic()`.

```{r}
library(symbolic)
f <- as_symbolic(function(x, y) log(2*x + 1 + y))
f
```

Symbolic functions are transformed with `derivative()`, `integral()` and
`solve()`. Each takes the argument to work with as a bare name, and returns a
new symbolic function.

```{r}
derivative(f, x)
integral(f, x)

# Solve log(2*x + 1 + y) == 0 for x
solve(f, 0, x)
```

`solve()` returns one column per solution, so its results always return a
matrix. Without `b`, it returns the inverse function, as `base::solve()` does
for matrices.

```{r}
solve(as_symbolic(function(x) exp(x)))
solve(as_symbolic(function(x) x^2), y, x)(c(1, 4, 9))
```

Since the results are ordinary R functions, they can be evaluated directly.

```{r}
derivative(f, x)(2, 1)
```

Definite integrals drop the variable of integration, as the result no longer
depends on it. Bounds are bare R expressions, which may be infinite or refer to
the other arguments.

```{r}
g <- as_symbolic(function(x, y) x^2 + x * y)
integral(g, x, lower = 0, upper = 1)
integral(g, x, lower = 0, upper = y)
integral(as_symbolic(function(x) exp(-x^2)), x, lower = -Inf, upper = Inf)
```

Every name in a bound is a symbol, and symbols which aren't already arguments
become arguments of the result. Use `!!` to inject the value of a variable
instead. A bound can even mention the variable of integration, so integrating a
density up to `x` gives its cumulative distribution function.

```{r}
dens <- as_symbolic(function(x, rate) rate * exp(-rate * x))
support_min <- 0
integral(dens, x, lower = !!support_min, upper = q)
integral(dens, x, lower = 0, upper = x)
```

Transformations compose, so they can be chained together.

```{r}
f |>
  derivative(x) |>
  solve(y, x)
```

The same rules apply to `solve()`'s right hand side as to bounds: every name is
a symbol, which is why `y` above is solved against rather than evaluated. Names
which aren't already arguments of the function become arguments of the result.

`deriv()` works as it does for `stats::deriv()`, returning a function whose
value carries its gradient (and optionally Hessian) as attributes, but it can
differentiate any function Maxima can.

```{r}
deriv(f, hessian = TRUE)(1, 0)
```

## Related work

`symbolic` is a thin functional interface over
[maxima](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/maxima), which exposes
[Maxima](https://maxima.sourceforge.io/) expressions directly. Use `maxima` if
you want to work with symbolic *expressions*; use `symbolic` if you want to work
with R *functions* and get R functions back.

To keep `symbolic` suitable as a low-level dependency, it does not mask any base
or `stats` functions. In particular `stats::integrate()` is left untouched, so
numerical integration continues to work as usual after attaching `symbolic`.
